message:
MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
## Lippage

Lippage is when one tile's edge sits slightly higher than the tile next to it, so the floor has tiny steps instead of being flat. You can feel it underfoot, it catches dirt and toes, and it shows up badly when light comes in low across the floor.

It's more common with long rectangular tiles like yours, because they're often very slightly bowed in the middle. Two things help a lot:
- **Tile levelling clips**: cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets.
- **Offsetting rows by a third of a tile, not half**: that avoids lining up the high middle of one tile with the edge of the next.

## Grout colour

For pale grey porcelain, go for a **mid grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. It blends in, and it won't show dirt the way white or very pale grout does within weeks. Very dark grout can look stripy against a pale tile.

A **stain-resistant grout** (most brands do one), or sealing standard grout after it cures, makes a big difference on a bathroom floor. Before committing, grout between two spare tiles and let it dry. Grout dries lighter than it looks in the tub.

## Toilet: before or after?

**Tile first, then fit the toilet.** The toilet then sits on the finished floor, the waste connection is set to the right height, and there are no awkward cuts around the base. It also means there are no gaps showing if you change the toilet later.

## How many boxes?

**Buy 4 boxes (32 tiles).**
- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- Each tile is 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18 m², so you need **24 tiles** to cover it
- Adding 10% gives 26.4, which rounds up to **27 tiles**
- 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4 boxes, so **4 boxes**

That leaves you about 8 spare tiles, more than 10%, which is good for a first job: you'll probably spoil a couple of cuts, and the toilet cut-out uses tiles too. Check that all the boxes have the same batch number so the shade matches, and keep a couple of spares afterwards for any future repair.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi [names],
>
> Just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor on Saturday morning, roughly [9am–12pm], so there may be some noise. Sorry about that, and thank you for being so patient with the skip on the drive these past couple of weeks. We really appreciate it, and it should all be done soon!
>
> [Your names, house number]

## Three beginner tips

1. **Get the base right before anything else.** The floor must be solid, clean and flat; tiles show every dip and bounce. On floorboards you'll need plywood or tile backer board screwed down first. Use a flexible adhesive suited to porcelain; the tub will say "S1" or "flexible".
2. **Dry-lay the tiles before you mix any adhesive.** Lay them out loose and plan where the cut tiles will fall. Aim to keep full tiles at the doorway, where they're most visible, and avoid thin slivers at any wall. Mark a straight starting line rather than trusting the walls to be square, because they usually aren't.
3. **Work in small sections and don't rush.** Mix small batches of adhesive and spread only about 1 m² at a time. For tiles this size, also spread a thin layer on the back of each tile ("back-buttering") so there are no hollow spots. Use the levelling clips, and lift a tile now and then to check it's fully covered underneath. Then keep off the floor until the adhesive has fully set.

The videos make it look easy because they're edited. Going slowly, especially on the first few rows, is completely normal. Good luck!
